a-j-norris-no-mans-land.A1:
Murdered for Money.
Eugene Brusher, a cattleman of Rush Center and well known in this city, was shot and killed Sunday, near No-man's-land, south of Dodge City, by a man named Marsh. From what we can learn, it seems that the two men left Dodge City together for Noman's-land and when near the state line his murderer shot him in the back, the ball passing through his heart, killing him instantly. Brusher left home with over seven hundred dollars. It is rumored that the murderer has been caught and hung and that over a hunderd dollars was found on his person. Another rumor has it that he was killed in a saloon. The remains of the murdered man arrived in this city from Dodge City,yesterday, to be shipped up the branch to his home in Rush Center.

POSTMASTER GENERAL DICKINSON has entered into a new contract with the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad company for fast mail service between Chicago and Council Bluffs to take effect March 13. The new contract is for daily service both east and west upon a schedule of fourteen and one-half hours. By this arrangement California mail leaving San Francisco in the evening after business hours and arriving at Council Bluffs in the afternoon of the third day will be taken up by the new fast train and will reach Chicago in time for the first morning delivery on the fourth day from the Pacific coast.

MRS. MARY HUNTER, who arrived from England lately, was not allowed to land at Philadelphia. Her son-in-law, Richard McCarney, said to the inspector that he had married in England, and that his mother-in-law, Mrs. Hunter, had persecuted him so that he fled to America. He sent for his wife and child, and his mother-in-law, Mrs. Hunter, accompanied them over, against their protest. McCarney said that she, Mrs. Hunter, was without means of support, and he refused to support her. The inspector refused to allow her to land.

A Kansan Murdered in No Man's Land.

LARNED, KAN., February 9.—Facts that have been developing for a da yor two, bring to light another bloody murder in the north end of No Man's Land. Eugene Brushers was a young man about 28 years old and lived at Walnut City, Rush county. He owned considerable property and was engaged in the cattle business. Some days ago he left on a business trip west, and nothing more was heard of him until his family received a telegram, last Saturday, stating that his body was at Dodge City to await further orders. Thomas McDowell, of Walnut City, passed through here Monday, en route to the scene of the murder. He returned this afternoon bringing the remains with him and reported the following facts:

Brushers arrived in Dodge City several days ago in company with a man who gave his name as Morris and his residence at Ness City. They were leading a gray stallion and were riding in a light spring wagon drawn by two black horses. The only firearms they appeared to have with them were a Winchester rifle and a 38-calibre pistol. Brushers claimed the wagon and horses, and they appeared to be good friends looking over the country. They finally left for Beaver City, in No Man's Land, about sixty miles south. On the way it was afterwards learned that the gray stallion was traded for a Texas pony. Nothing more was heard of the party until Sunday afternoon, when M. L. Kramer arrived at Dodge City from that country, bringing the dead body with him. He said that Brushers was shot at Beaver City on Friday, February 3, and it was supposed that Morris, his companion, was his murderer. These are the only facts that so far have come to light.
a-j-norris-no-mans-land.A13:
Brusher Revenged.
A special to the Wichita Eagle of the 18th, from Beaver City, No-Man's- Land, reports a sensational killing at that place last night. On February 10, Eugene Brusher was shot and killed by John Clark, who claimed that the shooting was accidental. The trial resulted in a verdict of criminal carelessness, and after heavily fining Clark for disturbing the peace, he was set free. In the meantime George Brusher, a brother of the murdered man, came here to investigate the affair. He and Clark apparently became chums, but last night Brusher shot and killed Clark and escaped to Kansas.
a-j-norris-no-mans-land.A15:
Criminal.
A. J. Morris, who murdered J. B. Brusher, in No Man's Land, was captured by a mob and hanged to a rafter in the principal saloon of the town.

I. S. Simon, a prominent citizen of St. Paul, Minn., was murdered and robbed in the hall of the Davidson Block, where he had rooms.

The police claim to have a clew to the burglar who murdered A. J. Snell in his home in Chicago and they are now on his track.

August Hotzke, of Chicago, charged with beating his stepson to death with a strap, has been found guilty of murder in the first degree and the jury recommended hanging.

Henry Fagte has been arrested at Leaf River, Ogle county, Ill., on the charge of stealing six head of cattle belonging to John Kaufman. The stock was sold in Rockford January 26.

Billy O'Connors, postoffice robber, and Frank St. Clair and William Thomas highwaymen, sawed their way out of the County Jail at St. Paul, Minn., Sunday evening, lowering themselves from the roof with ropes made of lammocks.

A young man of 19 named Hacker, of Danville, Ill., shot and killed a young lady of 18 named Steike, of Bell Plaine, Iowa, at the home of the latter's grandfather at Berlin, Wis., Monday night, and then shot himself. It was the result of unrequited affection.

Oliver P. Truett, of York, Pa., shot his wife three times Wednesday morning. Part of her tongue was taken off by one of the shots, and she was otherwise seriously injured. Truett then went up stairs and shot himself in the head.

Alonzo Holly (colored), imprisoned at Pinckneville, Ill., on a charge of assaulting a white woman, was taken from jail early Tuesday morning by six men and hanged to a tree.

At Washington early Tuesday morning Mrs Irene Park, the insane wife of a house-painter, attempted to kill her two children, and was only restrained after a desperate struggle with her husband. She used a hatchet on one of the children badly cutting her head, and attempted to cut the throat of the other with a dull case-knife.

night Constable S. P. Barger arrived in this city with Arthur Burton, a mulatto aged about eighteen, brother-in-law of Minor Jackson, of Brownsville. The charge against him was that of having committed rape on Eliza Harrington, aged about sixteen, a piece of Mrs. Ziner, with whom she had been living. The story of the girl was that he entered her room Friday night, told her he would kill her if she made any noise, chloroformed her, and committed the act. He was arrested Monday, taken before Squire Averill Tuesday, waived examination, was placed under $1000 bonds, and brought to this city as stated. BOARD OF TRADE.—The regular monthly meeting of the Board of Trade was held at the G. A. R. hall last Tuesday, about twenty members being present. A communication was read from the Portland News proposing to illustrate the city in a 65,000 edition of the paper for $300, or write it up for $50 a column. Laid on the table. The committee on preparing matter for an immigration circular asked further time, which was granted. After considerable discussion as to whether the circular should contain advertisements the committee was instructed to ascertain what portion of the cost of the circular could be paid by advertisements. The committee on a place for meeting reported that the G. A. R. hall could be had for $2 for regular meetings and $2.50 for special meetings, and the committee was ordered to make a contract for the cost of a salary for secretary and treasurer. Notice was given of a proposed amendment to the constitution providing for a committee of three on advertising and immigration and changing the time of meetings from Monday to Tuesday evenings. An adjournment was had until Tuesday evening next, when the committee on the immigration circular will report.

A COMLEY JOKE.—Some few days since a stranger arrived in the city, and, meeting Cap. Humphrey, asked that gentleman if one J. B. Comley resided in the city. On being informed that he did, the stranger asked Cap to introduce him to that gentleman, which Cap in his most suave and genteel manner proceeded to do. The stranger conversed with Mr. Comley for awhile and parted with him but met him the next day, and renewed the acquaintanceship of the day previous by conversing upon general topics, when Mr Comley incidently remarked that he had come from the State of Maine and named the town, whereupon the stranger stated that he had been in that town quite often, so the conversation turned upon their acquaintances in that place and they learned that they were mutually acquainted with many of the citizens of the down east burg. The stranger was in the town several days, and quite often met Mr. Comley with whom he held interesting conversations about the people in the far off city of his nativity. Finally it leaked out that the stranger was the youngest brother of Mr. Comley who at no time had had the least suspicion of the stranger's identity, J. B. acknowledged the "certainly" and set it up liberally for the "boys."

A SUGGESTION.—The Commencement exercises at the College last week completely demonstrated the fact that the chapel is entirely inadequate as a place in which to hold commencement exercises. This suggests the propriety of erecting at some time in the future a hall on the College grounds for such a purpose. A cheap, plain building, so arranged that it could be used for a gymnasium, if thought proper, would answer all purposes. The growing importance of our College as an educational institution makes it necessary to keep up with the times. The proper place to hold commencement exercises is in the College buildings, which makes such a hall as suggested the more a necessity. Some of the most lasting monuments that have been built have been College Halls for special purposes. Sibley Hall, at Cornell, for instance, and just now would be a fine opportunity for some Oregon man to leave a monument here that would cost but little. For instance, how would Corbitt Hall sound, or——Hall, after some Linn county man. Or, in time the usual method might be resorted to. The matter is worth thinking about.

LEBANON.—Lebanon is near the edge of the foothills, about 14 miles east of Albany. The population at this time is about 700. The surrounding country is a fine grain growing section. It has good public schools, and supports the Santiam Academy, an excellent school under the auspices of the M. E. Church. Lebanon is connected with Albany by a branch of the O. & C. R. R., and the Narrow Gauge road passes within three miles. Fine and extensive flouring mills are located here, grinding upwards of 50,000 bushels of wheat yearly. The power is obtained from the South Santiam by means of a canal, which proceeds to Albany, furnishing water power for the mills there. Lebanon is a flourishing town.—“Resources of Oregon.”

Declared Not Insane.
Eliza Harrington, the victim of the alleged Brownsville outrage, was taken before Justice Humphrey and a board of examining physicians yesterday afternoon and examined as to her sanity. TOLD BY CORRESPONDENTS
BROWNSVILLE.
Prof. B. F. Childers returned from Portland on Monday.

Joseph Blakely, Sheriff of Gillam county, visited family friends during the past week.

Miss Maud Hume on Thursday departed for Portland, from where she will proceed to New Tecoma, W. T., to visit her uncle.

The case of Albert Barton, who was arrested on a charge of rape, and in default of $1,000 bonds was taken to Albany for safe keeping, has created much comment in this section. As the defendant waived examination before Justice Averill, nothing other than floating reports are known of the innocence or guilt of the accused party. The facts of the case will probably be fully established at the proper time and place. The most exaggerated reports have gained circulation in regard to this affair, and seemingly without foundation, as there has been no evidence given as yet in the matter, public opinion being divided in regard to the guilt or innocence of the arrested party; the report of the attempted lynching of the prisoner is without foundation, the citizens of this place being willing to give the accused a fair and impartial trial and abide by the decision of the law.

Mrs. S. P. Barger, during the recent muddy spell, slipped and sustained a very severe sprain of the ankle.

The children of Elias Hall, four in number, who were ill from scarlet fever are all making rapid strides toward recovery, having fortunately passed the crisis of this dreaded disease in a most satisfactory manner.

O. H. Irvine, of Albany, was in town on Wednesday last attending to legal business.

Miss Annie Younger, a pupil of the Sacred Heart Academy of Salem, is passing the vacation months with her adopted parents, Mr. and Mrs. Hugh Fields, of South Brownsville.

J. W. Geary, M. D., of Halsey, was in town on professional business on Thursday last.

Ddward McKinney, of Arlington, Ore., who has been visiting relatives in Brownsville, returned home on Monday.

On Friday night the Brownsville woolen mills closed down for the space of two weeks, during which time the race will be cleaned and put in through repair.

A number of our citizens, taking advantage of the fine weather and low rates, participated in the excursion to Silverton on Saturday last.

The "Lash's Bitters" combination, during the past week visited our town, advertising their medicine and giving out-door concerts.

John Moore and James Simons have purchased building lots in Kirk's addition.

William Primley left Brownsville for Baker City during the past week.

Mrs. Lamson and daughter have for the past week been visiting town friends.

Wm. Robe departed for the Blue river mines on Monday last.

Work on the Lucky Boy mines, which has been temporarily suspended, will be resumed in a shot time.

Dan Howe is visiting his brother, J. M. Howe.

Rev. Samuel Driver, of Walla Walla, paid Brownsville relatives a visit, returning home on Saturday last.

Attorney D. R. N. Blackburn, of Albany, was in town on Saturday.

Portland, and was sitting near a rear window skylarking with some young men in the court below. bill-miles-1888-08.A10:
A BLOODY TRAGEDY.
Capt. Nat Kinney, Chief of the Bald Knobbers, Killed.
Springfield, Mo. August 26.—An-
Another terrible tragedy growing out of the late Bald Knob troubles has just been enacted in Christian County. Capt. Nat Kinney, the famous chief and founder of the Bald Knob organization, was last night shot and instantly killed at Ozark, by Bill Miles, an anti-Bald Knobber. Miles escaped and although pursued by an angry mob of fifty of Kinney's warmest supporters, has not yet been captured. Reliable particiblars of the tragedy have been received, but the correspondent's informant states that for more than two years Kinney and Miles had been at Daggers' point.

The feud originally arose in the troublesome times when Kinney was chief of the outlaw band and reigned the hills of Christian County with a rod of iron. Mills was bitter in his denunciation of the organization and when the law took a hand in the settlement of the troubles, he was most active in hunting evidence against members of the band. Saturday, the men attended a Republican rally at Ozark and remained over Sunday and yesterday. They quarreled once, but trouble was averted, and the friends of both tried to get them out of town.

Both refused to go and the town people looked for bloodshed, and they were not disappointed. Late at night the men met and the Bald-Knobber troubles were taken up and discussed by them. The argument grew into another quarrel, and suddenly both men drew their revolvers. Both men fired at about the same time, but Miles was a trifle the quickest and his ball was sent crushing through Kinney's brain. The giant Bald Knobber staggered, and then fell dead, with his brains and blood forming a pool around him.

Another report is that Kinney was shot from ambush but men who know Miles call him a square man, not capable of such a cowardly act. Intense excitement prevails in the vicinity of the murder and bloodshed is feared, as Kinney has an almost unanimous following in the hills. Among the rough people there he was king, and his kindly acts to men of his kind had endeared him to them.

His word was law, and the death of their chief will not go unavenged. A message has been sent to Harrison, Ark., for blood-hounds to track the murderer, and the horrible scenes that will follow have probably never been equalled in the Bald Knob hills.

A late message from Ozark confirms the killing of Capt. Kinney and the reports of the terrible excitement there. Capt. Kinney, the murdered chieftain, stood 6 feet 2 inches in his stocking feet and weighed 200 pounds. He was the founder of the organization, and from the fall of 1884 to the spring of 1887, was king of the boldest band of outlaws that ever disgraced the Southwest. His first individual murder was the killing of Andrew Coghorn at a church near Ozark on Sunday, March 12, 1886. After this repeated outrages and crimes were charged to him and his death is received with joy by the anti-Knoblers, and with feelings bordering on frenzy by members of the old band.

The following has been issued from the executive office:

Proclamation by the President of the United States: Constant thanksgiving and gratitude are due from the American people to Almighty God for His goodness and mercy which have followed them since the day He made them a nation and vouchsafed them a free government. With loving kindness He has constantly led us in the way of prosperity and greatness. He has not visited with swift punishment our shortcomings, but with gracious care He has warned us of our dependence upon our forbearance, and has taught us that obedience to His holy law is the price of a continuance of His precious gifts.

In acknowledgement of all that God has done for us as a nation, and to the end that on an appointed day the united prayers and praise of a grateful country may reach the throne of grace, I, Grover Cleveland, President of the United States, do hereby designate and set apart Thursday, the 29th day of thanksgiving and prayer, to be kept and observed throughout the land. On that day let all our people suspend their ordinary work and occupations, and in their accustomed places of worship, with prayer and songs of praise, render thanks to God for all his mercies; for the abundant harvests which have rewarded the toil of the husbandman during the year that has passed and for the rich rewards that have followed the labors of our people in their shops and their markets of trade and traffic. Let us give thanks for the peace and social order and the contentment within our borders, and for our advancement in all that adds to national greatness.

And, mindful of the afflictive dispensation with which a portion of our land has been visited, let us, while we humble ourselves before the power of God, acknowledging His mercy in setting bounds to the deadly march of pestilence, and let our hearts be chastened by sympathy with our fellow-countrymen who have suffered and who mourn. And, as we return thanks for all the blessings we have received from the hands of our Heavenly Father, let us not forget that he has enjoined upon us charity; and on this day of thanksgiving let us generously remember the poor and needy, so that our tribute of praise and gratitude may be acceptable in the sight of the Lord.

A JUDGMENT AFFIRMED.—The Court in General Term this morning decided the case of Jos. Reynolds agt. F. H. Smith et al., Judge Merrick delivering the opinion of the court. In this case a writ of attachment was served on the Columbia National bank as garnishee, and the defendant claimed that the court had no jurisdiction to issue the writ. The court holds on this claim that the rule of the court on the subject was made under authority and was a sound rule, and the court had, therefore, jurisdiction. The second objection, that the writ was not properly drawn, the court held untenable. The service was made on the cashier, and answer was made under the seal of the bank and by its full name. The third objection, that the funds attached were not the funds of Smith & Son, but were the funds of their clients, the court said, was the most important one. Public policy forbids the trustee from coming in himself and claiming the funds, but the true owner has such right. If the true owner stands by and does nothing then it is the court's duty to withdraw its hand and allow the condemnation of the credits. The judgment below was affirmed.

Thomas made no denial of the fact that he had the chicken, and said he tied it in his house to prevent it from fighting with his rooster. He said he did not tie his own rooster because he could not catch it. The judge thought he should not have tied the other man's rooster and not his own, and fined him $5.

FINED FOR STEALING COAL. — "Please to yo' honor, give me bail," is the manner in which Isaac Wood, an old colored man, addressed Judge Miller this morning. The old man was charged with stealing some coal from a car on the Baltimore and Ohio railroad. He was arrested by Detective Wirtz, who caught him in the act of stealing the coal. The old man denied taking any coal from the cars, but admitted that he picked up some which had dropped along the track. "What did you want with the coal?" asked the judge. At a church in an adjoining county on Sunday morning just before preaching, a crowd of farmers were seated in the shade of a large oak discussing matters relative to their noble avocation. By some hook or crook, the credit system was introduced and fully discussed by all, save one old gentleman who kept "mum." He was noted far and wide as being one of the most eccentric fellows in all the land and his comrades prevailed on him for his views.

"Well men," he said, "I'll tell you what I think about it in a mighty short time. I'll give you my personal experience. Last year I was living with you as you remember. Well I went up to W—— and found a man willing to run me. I tell you I lived high. He actually fed me—furnished my clothes, fed my stock—supplied me with tobacco; and would you believe it, really let me have sugar and coffee and shoes—everything and nary a time did he cheap "money" to me. Thus it went on during the spring, summer and early fall. Oh, I rolled in clover. But when the leaves begun to turn and about the time for the autumnal equinox to come on, a genuine commercial cyclone struck me and scattered corn, cotton, potatoes, wheat, oats, mules, horses, cows, calves, pigs—lock, stock and barrel—and bore it away. It went away in wagons. Yes, sir, he run me in the spring and summer and everlastingly galloped me in the fall. Run me out of the county. From now henceforth and forever I don't want no more running in mine—a fox trot will do me. If the merchant is satisfied I am."

A gentleman whose word is undoubted for truth, reports that, while squirrel hunting the other evening on the ridge between James Garrett's and Ed Carlock's, he discovered a small hole in the ground near a bunch of hickory sprouts, and, as he thought, yellow jackets going in and coming out, but on examination he found them to be bees. After considering a short time over the matter, he concluded to make a thorough search after their whereabouts, therefore he went a short distance to a neighbor's house, procured a pick and shovel and returned, commenced digging and excavating the dirt and soon he struck honey in vast quantities. A sensation was created at two o'clock in Augusta, Tuesday, by the report, which rapidly gained circulation, that young Frank Wheless had killed himself. A crowd of his friends soon collected before the front door of the wholesale house of Wheless & Co., on Warren block.

The lifeless body of young Wheless was found in a pool of blood in his bed in the sleepingroom above the store. A 38-calibre pistol was grasped in his right hand, one chamber of which had been discharged. The bullet had entered just above the right ear and had torn its way entirely through his head, coming out on the left side near the top. When the shot was fired Mr. W. T. Wheless, Frank's father, was in an adjoining room. He thought the shot came from downstairs, and rushed down into the store. Finding no one there, he ran out on the pavement and then back in the store, to be greeted by the shocking discovery that his son had killed himself.

A note was left asking the delivery of certain little keepsakes, but there was nothing ascribing or indicating any cause for the rash act. Frank Wheless was a popular and successful young business man, and there was nothing in the condition of his affairs to warrant his action. He attended to his duties about the store as usual in the morning. At one time he was sitting in a rocking chair, and seemed moody, drowsy and quiet. His father remarked that he seemed sleepy, and he replied, "yes, I didn't sleep well last night."

He was last seen alive by Mr. Will Harris, a young man employed in the store. His room adjoined Frank's, and they went up together to get ready for dinner. Frank sat on the bedside and moved a pillow that was lying at the foot of the bed, and placed it at the head. In doing so he exposed the pistol, which was under the pillow. He leaned over, and picking up the pistol, placed it under the pillow at the head of the bed, laid back upon it with his feet hanging over the bedside, and one resting on the floor. In this attitude Harris left him when he went out to dinner, and thus he was found when the pistol shot was heard. His pulse beat for several minutes, but death soon came. So far as his consciousness was concerned, death was instantaneous. Frank Wheless came home from Birmingham a few months ago, where he had been in the real estate business, to go into business with his father. He was a joyous, light-hearted fellow, and a good business man. The jury returned a verdict of death by a pistol shot wound from his own hands.

Mr. Frank Davis, residing near Fairburn, on last Wednesday, upon going to the house from the field, Wednesday, found his little three year old child sitting in the door crying and when asked what it was crying for, it replied that its mother was gone. Tuesday, at Canton, Mrs. Gober was feeling badly and thought she would take paregoric to relieve her suffering. By mistake she took up a vial of medicine which Dr. Turk had left with her some months ago to be given the baby in small doses, and drank a large swallow out of it. She at once realized a burning, tingling sensation and went down stairs to see her mother about it. As she turned to go up the steps she found her limbs were becoming benumbed and it was with difficulty she ascended the stairs. She soon grew worse and becoming alarmed sent for Dr. Coleman, who came at once, and, after making a hurried examination, found that she had taken a large dose of a deadly poison and that it would be next to impossible to save her, as the poison had been taken upon an empty stomach and had become well digested. In about two hours after he was called in she died in great agony with convulsions. She and her three little children were living with her mother, Mrs. Sarah A. Johnson, at Canton. Mr. Gober is working in the mines of Colorado, and has not been home in several months. Mrs. Gober was not quite twenty-two years old.

Tuesday evening last Elisha Pruce, a white man, who three months ago quit his wife and left her and family, near Swainesboro, returned and asked her to live with him again, which she refused to do. He then wanted pay for some guano which he claimed to have furnished her to use on her farm. She refused to pay, and he left very angry. That night he procured a pistol, and going back the next morning, saw her, hoe in hand, hoeing some cotton. Without saying one word, he commenced shooting at her, missing the first time. He shot again, this time hitting her in the hand. She broke and ran, and he shot again, missing her.

He then ran and caught her, throwing her down and shooting two bullet holes through her head, and her brains run out all on the ground. The pistol he used was a 38-calibre Smith & Wesson. The news spread rapidly, and the coroner of Emanuel county, James M. Cowart, was sent for. When he arrived to hold the inquest over the remains of the woman, he was sent for about half a mile to hold an inquest over Elisha Pruce himself, he having taken strychnine and killed himself. The bottle with the poison was found by him, half of it gone, and the pistol with which he shot his wife was found in his hand. The post mortem, held by Dr. George L. Smith, developed the fact of the poisoning.

This ordeal, however, had been so long continued and was such a terrible strain upon Mr. Sharp's mind that when rescued he, too, was but a raving maniac. His mind seemed entirely gone, though formerly he was a man of strong mind, used to dealing with insane people are familiar with their curses and threats. He was taken to Englewood, Kan., in a wagon, with hands and feet tied. A NEGRO LYNCHED.
A SENSATION IN THE YOUNG TOWN OF BESSEMER, ALA.
Handy Posey Is Hanged By a Mob for Having Attempted to Ravish a Twelve-Year-Old White Girl—Great Excitement.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., April 24.—The most noteworthy thing that daylight discovered to the citizens of the little city of Bessemer this morning was the dead body of a 150-pound negro suspended from an oak tree in the center of the town, placarded: "Our inothers, wives and daughters must and shall be protected." The fact of the negro's "removal," however, was not news to many of those who looked upon his dead body. It was accomplished about midnight last night by a masked mob, after they had dragged him through the town, shouting: "Lynch him!" "String him up!"

Handy Posey was the negro's name. His offense was the attempted raping of Mamie McKinney, a twelve year old white girl, adopted daughter of a mechanic living just out of the town whose surname she bore. The assault took place at McKinney's home last Friday afternoon. The girl broke from Posey's grasp in time to save herself, and McKinney, who had been attracted to the spot by her cries, gave chase to him and caught him in the heart of the town where he was turned over to the police. The matter of lynching the prisoner was mooted that night but was left in abeyance awaiting further proofs of his identity. Saturday several negroes were ranged in front of the girl and she unhesitatingly spotted Posey as her assailant. Plans were laid forth with to make way with him, but he was so well guarded at the lockup that it was not thought advisable to try to take him. Yesterday, however, the marshal thinking his house would be the safest place for the prisoner over night, took him there, and it was there that the avengers took him last night. The mob made the marshal and the two policemen of the town go along with them and see the work well done. Mamie McKinney says she was in the yard Friday afternoon when Posey came by and asked: "Have you seen any horses around here?" She replied she had not, but the negro lingered near and finally she asked him what he wanted. He approached her from behind and grabbing her about the waist said he'd kill her if she made any noise and threw her to the ground. But Mamie did scream lustily and finally broke away from him.

Raping seems to run in the Posey family. Handy, who was twenty-one years old, was a young brother of Wesley Posey, who raised such a racket here in December, 1883, by a similar attempt on a five-year-old white child. Half of the Second Alabama regiment was required here for nearly a week to protect him from the populace. He was convicted under guard of the troops and sentenced to hang, but the supreme court remanded the case because he was denied a change of of venue and awaiting trial in an adjoining county. He died in jail here.

A NEGRO ASSAULTS A LITTLE GIRL
A Mob Takes Charge of Him and Hangs Him to a Limb-Threats of Vengeance.
A Mob Takes Charge of Him and Hangs Him to a Limb—Threats of Vengeance.

Hardy Posey, colored, was lynched by a mob of masked white men for attempt to rape a twelve year old white girl at Bessemer, Ala.

The negro went to the home of a farmer named McKinney, who lives just outside of town. He found Alice McKinney, a twelve year old girl, alone, and approaching her from behind, threw her to the ground and attempted to outrage her. Her screams brought her uncle to the rescue, and the negro ran, but was soon caught. He was taken in charge by the police and was locked up. The girl was brought in

AND IDENTIFIED POSEY

in a crowd of twenty negro men. There was no excitement, but a determination to make swift and certain punishment was seen in the faces of the white men of the town.

The town marshal took the prisoner to his residence and placed him under strong guard, but his precautions were useless. Soon after midnight two hundred masked men appeared at the officer's house and demanded the prisoner.

The men were very quiet and had little to say, but they meant business. Posey was taken, and the officers were compelled to go along with the mob and see the work well done. About fifty feet from the depot, near the center of the town, stood a large oak tree, and under this the crowd stopped. The negro was bound hand and foot and the rope placed around his neck with the regulation hangman's knot. A large placard was pinned to his breast, bearing the words:

"Our mothers, wives and daughters must and shall be protected.

[Signed]

"BESSEMER'S BEST CITIZENS."

The leader then gave the order to pull away, and in a moment the negro's body was hanging from a limb, his feet being ten feet from the ground. The crowd then moved away as quietly as they came.

The body was left

HANGING TO THE LIMB

until 9 o'clock in the morning, when it was cut down by the coroner.

Posey was a brother of Wesley Posey, who came near sharing the same fate at the hands of a mob in Birmingham four years ago. Wesley Posey assaulted a white woman, and the efforts of a mob to lynch him brought about the "Posey riot" at Birmingham, and caused all the State troops to be ordered there. He was afterwards tried and convicted, but died in jail soon after being sentenced.

Cardinal Ireland.

Since the return of Bishop Ryan from Rome a rumor has gained currency in church circles that another Cardinal's hot will come to America at no distant day. The names of the dignitary upon whom this high ecclesiastical honor will be conferred has not leaked out, but a prominent priest, who is in the closest confidence with Bishop Ryan, in speaking of the matter, gave it as his opinion that if the report is true, Archbishop Feehan, of Chicago, or Bishop Ireland, of Minnesota, who has just been created an archbishop, will be selected. Listing Iron Stocks.

The Minnesota Iron company, of Duluth, has just made application to the New York stock exchange for the listing of its stock there for transfer. The company, under its reorganization, is capitalized at $14,000,000. This, including the Duluth and Iron Range railway, the docks at Two Harbors, the mines at Tower and many thousand acres of iron lands along the range. It is an unusual thing for an iron company to list its stocks on the exchange to be placed regularly on the market, but it is undoubtedly a good move and one that will resound to the advantage of the company and the entire Vermillion region.

The beauties of the jury system were well illustrated in the court of general sessions in New York recently. Kittie Mulhern appeared as complainant in a breach of promise case against John Johnston, a colored man. Her testimony was enough to prove that she wanted very much to marry the negro, but it by no means proved that the latter had promised to accommodate her. Summary Punishment.

On the border of Claiborne and Caplah counties, in Mississippi, near Port Gibson, a negro named James Hicks attempted to outrage a little colored girl, 7 years old. The child complained to her parents and the fiend was pursued and captured by the father, who had him tied to a tree and administered 200 lashes on his bare back, then turned loose and ordered to leave the country. The colored people of the neighborhood were not satisfied with the punishment, and determined to lynch the brute. Hicks in the meantime had armed himself with an adze, and when set upon by the negroes he split the head of one open, knocked down another and made a break for liberty, when his race was cut short by a load or two of buckshot. He was then dragged to a tree some distance from where he was shot, hung up and left there. The first intimation the white people had of the deed was the finding of the hanging body the next morning.

A sculling match recently took place at Sydney, N. S. W., between Peter Kemp, of Australia, and Edward Hanlan, of Canada. Kemp won by five lengths. The race was rowed over the Paramatta course. Kemp took the lead at the start. Hanlan's boat came in contact with that of his opponent before the mile post was reached. Kemp stopped and let Hanlan pass, and then went after him. Realizing the enormity of his offence Wooldridge turned and fled. Many persons pursued him as he took his rapid course over Church Hill and down to the river-bank below Gillie's creek. Here he darted under the wharf—the second one below Gillie's creek—and was lost to the sight of the crowd which had followed him and those other persons who had gathered from that immediate neighborhood.

THE SEARCHERS.

From the First police-station Sergeants Whitlock, Howard, and Matthews, and Policemen Robert Brown, John Brown, Parkinson, Curl, Kerse, and Holdscraft were sent down, and with lanterns they set diligently to work to discover where Wooldridge was concealing himself. The work was an extremely difficult one, especially after darkness came on, and Policeman Holdscraft in the earnestness of his endeavors made a false step and fell into the mud and water, doing himself no great damage, but seriously marring the appearance of his suit.

HE COMES OUT.

Some time about 9 o'clock Wooldridge broke from his cover and ran away from the wharf in the direction of the gasworks. He was naked, except that a strip of his drawers hung about his waist. He had gone about three squares when his course was checked by a colored man; but before that several shots had been fired at him. Now seeing himself surrounded by a great howling crowd armed with pistols, shotguns, and everything else that would kill or wound, Wooldridge was glad to find shelter with the police. He was out of breath, naked, and scared to death. There were a number of calls for "rope," the meaning of which was that the crowd believing, that the boy was dead, wanted to hang the murderer. But the police were too active and numerous for any successful demonstration of that sort.

HIS NAKEDNESS COVERED.

The street-car people were kind enough to furnish the police with a blanket. This they threw over the shivering wretch and took him to the First station-house. Here he was seated in a chair by the stove and a stiff drink of whiskey given him, and then he gave the name of Joe Wooldridge, and said that his age was twenty-six. Later he stated that he had been employed upon Captain John Edwards's oyster-boat until two weeks ago, when he was put off.

WOUNDED.

Seated by the stove, the blanket half off his shoulders. Wooldridge, who could not or would not speak much, pointed out that he was wounded. What appeared to be a bullet-mark was seen on the fleshy part of the arm near the right shoulder. Later, when he was put in a cell, Wooldridge stated that he was shot on Seventeenth street. This may be so, but some are of the opinion that he was shot at Rockets.

Wooldridge threw off much of his clothing in his flight; the remainder he rid himself of while under the wharf. Possibly his purpose was to swim the river if opportunity occurred, but he never got the chance, and for several hours was exposed to the cold. Under the wharf where he concealed himself there was little or no water.

The accused is a yellow-skinned man of medium size and seems to be well-knit and sinewy.

AN ACCOUNT OF THE CUTTING.

Mr. R. H. Pranzell, the father of the wounded boy, was seen by a Dispatch reporter last night about 11 o'clock at his residence. He is an employee of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway Company, and lives at No. 1005 north Seventeenth street, three doors north of Richards street, which is two squares beyond the grain elevator. "About 4 o'clock this afternoon," said he, "or soon after, while I was in Mr. Gifford's store, just at the corner below my house, Robert, my older boy, came in and told me that a colored man had his brother Emmet down and had almost killed him. I went out hastily and the boy had been released. I approached the negro and asked why he had seen fit to treat my little boy so roughly, and at the same told him that I always corrected my children when any of their misdeeds were reported to me. He mumbled something in reply, and all that I could hear was to the effect that the boys on this street interfered with the negro in passing. He turned his back on me and continued muttering something that I could not exactly understand. Just at this juncture Emmet stepped up by the side of the negro and the latter reached around and made two strikes at the boy. After the second my son slapped his hand to his abdomen, bent as if injured in the stomach, and screamed. At this the negro took to his heels and, realizing that my son had been badly cut, I followed the fugitive, and a number of others joined in the chase, including Mr. Wright, a friend of mine, who is a fireman on the road. We ran until my breath gave out and I fell to the pavement as if dead. Persons near by came to my assistance and used water and other restoratives, and in about fifteen minutes I regained consciousness and was brought home."

OUT OF HIS BOOTS.

"This," continued Mr. Branzell, "was near Oakwood, I think, but I really do not know. It was an entirely strange neighborhood to me. When on the hill the negro, seeing that I was gaining on him, ran into a house. Mr. Wright and I endeavored to gain admittance, but were refused. Finally, when we were at the side of the house, the negro, who had gotten out of his boots, ran out of the front-door and started off again in post-haste. We followed and I gained rapidly, but had not gotten far when I fell."

Nesterday afternoon Emmett Branzell
Yesterday afternoon Emmett Branzell, a young white man, and Joseph Wooldridge, a negro, had some words and a difficulty. Emmett reported the fact to his father, and together, about 4:30 o'clock, the two saw Wooldridge at the corner of Seventeenth and Price streets, two squares beyond the grain elevator. After the cutting Wooldridge ran and was pursued up over the hills, through Howard's Grove, and from there down to the dock where the steamer Norwood lands. A Horse Trader Murdered by His Companions in a Debauch.

LOUISVILLE, Oct. 6.—Near Mayfield, Ky., Harriet Hurd, an old colored woman, yesterday found in the woods the remains of William Trafford, a horse trader. Trafford's head was crushed as if by a heavy stick and his throat was cut. When the fact was reported an inquest was held. Suspicion pointed to John Carter, son of a Mayfield butcher who had been in Trafford's company the night before at a house of ill repute. Carter was found at Cold Water, twelve miles distant. An examining trial was begun, and the evidence of the woman showed that Carter had gone out with Trafford and returned alone, saying, "he had more money than sense," and also there were blood stains on Carter's clothes. THE POOR IN ENGLAND.

A Very Hard Winter in Prospect for Them.

London, Sept. 4.—The stout-hearted unphilosophical statisticians of England protest that they do not anticipate any extraordinary distress among the poor during the coming winter in consequence of the partial failure of the wheat crop here, necessitating the importation of an unusual quantity of breadstuff. To be sure the premises of these gentlemen, presumably situated very comfortably themselves, appeared to be based on that common quality of mind which enables us to bear the misfortunes of others with becoming resignation, but the same view of the matter appears to be taken by some of the leading metropolitan and provincial journals, notably the Times and the Manchester Guardian, and their views are probably the result of careful consideration.

It is true that the interests of England are so varied that a partial observer is apt to overlook many circumstances which go far to qualify what seems an indisputable calamity. The crops have failed, and the quantity of wheat to be imported is much larger than usual. The loss falls first upon the farmers and agricultural laborers, but the farmer appears to still subsist after being rained from year to year, and the latter with some little relief appear to get along in some manner.

The industrious poor of the great cities, miserable enough now, will feel the pressure, of course, more than the others. Bread has gone up and the hard struggle is intensified, but great efforts are being made to alleviate the condition of the worthy, and the brazen class, who seldom or never work, will live in their accustomed mode.

RALEIGH, Sept. 3.—A wholesale lynching such as was never before recorded in the history of the State, occurred yesterday morning at Oxford, in Granville county. At about 3 o'clock in the morning three negroes—Henry Tanner, his son, John Tanner, and Alonzo Smith—were taken from jail by a masked mob and hanged to a tree in the suburbs of the town. A NORTH CAROLINA LYNCHING.

RALEIGH, N. C., Sept. 5.—There was a very sensational lynching at Oxford, Granville county, Sunday, which ended the lives of three criminals who were hated by both whites and blacks. At 2 o'clock in the morning, while the town was at its quietest, about a hundred men, well mounted and particularly well disguised, rode in. They were evidently from the country, and it was plain that both white and colored people were in the party. They rode very quietly to the court house and jail, which are not far apart. They forced the door of the sheriff's office, and in a drawer of his desk found the keys to the steel cells of the jail. While one party was thus engaged others had forced the jail door and seized the jailer.

At this stage of the proceedings some noise was made which caused a policeman to approach. The lynching party at once seized him as they had the jailer and fastened him securely. The masked men then quickly opened the doors of the cells and took therefrom three colored men, Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith. This was done in good order and very systematically. The masked men had carefully picketed all approaches to the jail. When they had their prisoners secured the mob rode away in the darkness and everything became perfectly quiet.

The policeman ran to town and gave an alarm on a bell which is used as a signal for the assembling of the local military. The latter assembled, but when they got to the jail the mob had already left town with its victims, and there was nothing to do, as there was no clew to the lynchers.

In the morning the bodies of the bodies of all three men were discovered where they had been hanged.

An inquest was held, but nothing was done, and the jury therefore adjourned until the 6th inst. It will meanwhile seek for any evidence as to the identity of the lynchers.

John and Henry Tanner were in jail charged with killing 'Squire Grissom, an old colored man, in Granville county last June. The evidence that they were guilty was very positive. They had murdered him in order to get at some property belonging to him, and were aided by Lizzie Canaday and Dora Grissom, also colored.

They had beheaded Grissom with an ax and otherwise mangled him. He had been dead five days when found in the house. Feeling ran high against the four parties named, and all were soon jailed, the coroner's jury rendering a verdict of willful murder against the two men.

Smith the other man lynched, was held for arson and burglary, both capital crimes. Some other prisoners in the jail charged with poisoning a woman were not molested, though it had been feared they would be lynched. Several nights last week the military guarded the jail, but they were with-drawn last Wednesday, as there was no sign of an attempt to lynch.

Three Negroes Taken from the Oxford Jail and Hanged.
Three Negroes Taken from the Oxford Jail and Hanged.

Our citizens were startled Monday to learn that three persons had been lynched near Oxford Saturday night. They were all negroes, Henry and John Tanner, father and son, confined in Granville county jail for murdering an old colored man named, Squire Grissom, last June, and Alonzo Smith, waiting trial for burglaring and burning Mr. James Thomasson's dwelling house. The crime of the Tanners was a most diabolical one, and the community in which it was committed was justly outraged thereat. That of Smith was a very grave offense but not deserving of the swift and summary judgment that was visited upon him. The Tanners, if guilty, deserved the fate they met, but it ought to have come through the regular channels of the law. But there is the trouble. Too many scoundrels whose necks should be broken go unpunished through the slow process of the law, too long, or by one means or another escape altogether. The laxity of the law, the various technicalities by which the ends of justice are defeated, are more responsible for the lynchings that occur than anything else. It is this that causes an outraged and indignant people to resort to mob law. We do not believe it was any disregard of the law, but a want of respect for and confidence in it because of too frequent abuse, that caused those persons engaged in the affair to take three criminals from the jail in Oxford Saturday night and hang them. We do not believe the act was instigated from any love of mob violence; it was rather the promptings of a love for law and order.

The affair was a horrible one and is to be deplored, but the Gold Leaf charges that the law itself, or the ministers of the law, are responsible for it. Let a people know that crime will be punished by the courts, and they will not so often take matters of this kind in their own hands.

The lynching took place about two o'clock Sunday morning. The crowd, which was composed of both whites and blacks, came from the country and did their work quickly. The bodies were quietly buried and all is as quiet as though nothing had happened.

Poker Room in a Church Tower. LOUISVILLE, Ky., Feb. 19.—A regular poker room was discovered in the tower of the Walnut Street Presbyterian church here last night. The players were negroes who were let in the back way by the janitor and played steadily without reference to what was going on in the church below, which has one of the largest white populations in the city. When services were not in progress the negroes occasionally used the pews in the audience room for couches for weary gamesters, who were broken in the game and had no regular lodging place. Four Men Shot to Death in Louisiana.
JEANERETTE, La., Feb. 9.—In an altercation, George Dixon was shot and killed by Jake Marshall, colored, a deputy sheriff. Marshall fled and concealed himself in a corn crib, where he was found with his brother. The pair were fired upon, and the brother and Louis Payton were almost instantly killed. Payton was a spectator. Jake Marshall succeeded in escaping, but received fatal wounds, as was discovered when his dead body was found in a ditch in the swamps. The shooting was done by unknown persons.

Fooled With a Pistol.

AUGUSTA, Ky., Feb. 9.—While fooling with an old 38-caliber revolver, Jesse Newman, aged twenty-two, was fatally shot by Robert Daniels, aged eighteen years. The ball entered the right side just below the ribs, wounding the liver and the intestines, and, passing down, lodged against the pelvis on the opposite side. This occurred just below this place on the Ohio side. The wound is a fatal one. Newman exonerates Daniels from all blame.

His First Veto.

SALT LAKE, Utah, Feb. 9.—Governor West sent in his first veto yesterday. It was on a bill compelling the courts to grant bail in the case of convicts who wish to appeal where the penalty is not greater than five years' imprisonment. The law now allows bail in such cases in the discretion of the judge. The design of the bail was to help the polygamists fight the laws. The governor to-day signed the old appropriation bill.

He Just Loaned the County's Money.

MINNEAPOLIS, Minn., Feb. 9.—The Journal's Highmore, Dak., special says that Homer James, the Hyde county treasurer, who is $10,000 short in his accounts, has been discharged after an earnest prosecution. The cause of this action was that James was strictly honest and had not profited personally by the shortage. He had simply been good natured and lent county money to any friends who asked him, taking neither receipt nor note.

The town authorities has a force at work this morning scraping the streets of the mud that has accumulated during the winter. If this is done occasionally, Danville, instead of being a very dusty town during windy weather, will be just the reverse.

Dr. E. A. Grant, a noted specialist of Louisville, was in town several days last week. Mr. I. M. Dunn, late of Lebanon, who bought C. R. Anderson's interest in the mill business of Smith & Anderson, was in town Saturday. He will take charge May 1st.

Miss Mary Whitthorne has returned to her home in Columbia, Tenn., after a visit to her sister, Mrs. C. P. Cecil. Mrs. Ellen Cook, Miss Emma Cook and Mrs. C. P. Terhune attended the celebration of Rev. Strother Cook's golden wedding near Burgin on Thursday. Mr. Cook is a brother of the late Allen Cook.

The Boyle county jurors who gave Sidebottom, the Pulaski county murderer, a life sentence, say since their return home that they do not doubt but what the convicted man richly deserved hanging, but that under the strictly impartial ruling of Judge Morrow the confession was excluded and that with that left out only strong circumstances connecting Sidebottom with the murder could be gotten before the jury. As oftimes happens the officers who undertook to work up the case got entirely too "smart." After Sidebottom was arrested it is said that the officers in order to induce him to confess told him that it would be much better for him to do so, and even went so far as to tell him that they would go on his bond and that he could then leave the country if he would only confess. It is time that officers and all others should know that the law permits no such "shenanigan" with a person under duress and that Judge Morrow in protecting the rights of an ignorant individual, even though he be a red-handed murderer, is observing no more closely than he ought to do the law as he finds it and his oath of office.

As John Keel, a tenant living on Wm. Tandy's farm, near Hopkinsville, Ky., was helping to load a hegshead of tobacco on to a wagon, a few days since, it slipped and rolled over Keel, crushing him in a frightful manner and inflicting internal injuries from which he has since died.

Henry Miller shot at a crowd of women a few nights ago at South Pittsburgh, Tenn., who were laughing at him. Smith Langford, of Anniston, Ala., interfered and Miller shot him through the brain, killing him instantly. A general row followed, in which George Cook was fatally cut about the head and neck.

They had gathered, but as they were on the way to the jail the Methodist Church caught fire, and they stopped to help put it out. Meantime the jailer got word, and with his prisoner escaped.

A Montgomery (Ala.) restaurant boasts of a waiter who is a German baron.

Commander-in-Chief Rea of the G. A. R. was banqueted at Nashville, Tenn., both Federal and Confederate veterans participating.

Ten practicing physicians of Bartow, Fla., have written a letter in which they state that no yellow fever cases have been in existence in either the town or county.

The strawberry crop of Eastern Tennessee is ripening rapidly, and the growers are beginning to ship. The yield promises to be fair.

Fire destroyed the Louisiana Furniture and Coffin Manufacturing Company's establishment at New Orleans, entailing a loss of $40,000.

The City Court of Mobile, Ala., returned a verdict giving $25,000 damages to G. Hall, a brakeman, who had his foot cut off by a train on the Louisville & Nashville railroad.

Elder L. W. Welsh, pastor of the Christian Church at Hopkinsville, Ky., has tendered his resignation. He will go to Columbia, Mo., to accept a position as teacher there.

James Ford, of Simpson County, Ky., shot and fatally wounded Jim King, the marshal of Adairville, a few days ago. This is the third killing in that hamlet in the past year.

Tom Hanberry, Jr., formerly of Hopkinsville, Ky., was shot and instantly killed at Australia Landing, Miss., a few days ago.

The attorneys representing the $50,000 suit of Rev. Frederick Howard against three newspapers of Tennessee and sixteen members of the First Baptist Church of Nashville, have withdrawn from the suit. They decline to give any reason.

Chief Post-Office Inspector Gullich has received notice of the arrest of Theodore Loswell at Monroe, La., for robbing the Monroe post-office.

The weather in Virginia has been very cold for the season, and there have been some heavy frosts. Great anxiety is felt for the fruit. It is thought to be ruined in some localities.

While an engine on the Louisville, New Orleans & Texas railway was backing up Levee street to the depot at Vicksburg, Miss., to pull out the south-bound passenger train a few days ago, it ran over a two-year-old son of Mr. Joseph Stackner, crushing it so that it died in a few minutes.

I. I. Dorsey, Jr., the well-known trotting-horse breeder and turf writer, fell dead at his farm near Louisville, Ky., a few days ago, aged sixty-nine. For over thirty years he has bred fine trotters in this country. He founded the Gold Dust family. Epaulet sold for $22,500, and was probably the finest horse he ever trained. Dorsey was an Englishman and a graduate of Oxford.

R. F. Sullivan, of Rockingham County, Va., agent for J. P. Cooper, representative of foreign bondholders, of London, was recently indicted for selling Virginia coupons. During the term of the Circuit Court at Harrisburg, just adjourned, one hundred suits against parties for offering coupons in payment of State taxes were tried. Eighty-six judgments were rendered.

The dwelling-house of Louis Stromans, near Springfield, S. C., was burned a few mornings since and four of Stromans' children, two boys and two girls, who were sleeping up-stairs, perished in the flames. Stronmans' eldest son was frightfully burned while frantically endeavoring to rescue his brothers and sisters, and will probably die.

The business portion of the town of Harrellsville, in Hartford County, N. C., was burned a few days ago. An incendiary fired the restaurant of Geo. Baker, and the fire quickly spread to nine stores, all wooden structures, and burned them all, as well as a dwelling and the post-office. The loss is estimated at $75,000. There was considerable salvage of goods in the burned stores.

Judge Key, of the United States District Court, at Nashville, Tenn., has sentenced Arthur A. Stanton to twelve months' imprisonment and a fine of $500. Stanton was storekeeper and gauger, and while watching the distillery of J. C. Barnes, of Putnam County, let the owner have the keys to the bonded warehouse for the purpose of removing several barrels of whisky, the profits of which were to be equally divided.

Mrs. Holly Sheldon, of Graves County, Ky., at this writing had eaten nothing for fifty-six days. All this time she has been in apparent good health, being perfectly rational all the while and suffering no pain up to a few days ago. She says she merely lost her appetite, and has no desire to eat. The case is attracting great interest in the neighborhood, and medical men are at a loss to account for the strange affliction of the lady.

GENERAL SHERIDAN's continued prostration caused the most intense anxiety to his friends on the 26th, and an effort would immediately be made to remove him to Nonquitt, Buzzard's Bay, Mass.

"Uncle Dick," as he was commonly called, was an extraordinary man physically. He was near eighty years of age and never had a spell of sickness before. Has been on the mines around old Villa Rica for about fifty years, and the accident that befell him lately was the first that ever happened to him.

A party of negro gamblers, both sexes, who have been plying their trade at Glenmore, was reported to the authorities of Ware county by two respectable colored men named Grant and Parker. This incensed them to such a degree as that they armed themselves and swore vengeance against these men.

Monday night, with guns and pistols, they collected outside of a store in which Grant was setting, and sent one of their number in to assault him. The white men interfered in his behalf, and saved him from their clutches. Tuesday morning Constable McDonald attempted to arrest the ringleader of a mob that had collected, and menaced the peace of the town, when the negro reached for his hip pocket, whereupon the constable sent a bullet crashing through his shoulder, disabling him. Three more shots from the constable's trusty pistol succeeded in arresting the intended depredators of the mob, and eight of the leaders were arrested by Sheriff Henderson and a deputy, and safely lodged in Ware county jail at Waycross. All is now quiet at Glenmore.

News ereached here of the lynching of Ned Clark, colored, in Worth county. Clark was charged with attempting to commit a rape upon a young white girl thirteen years of age. His capturers were conveying him to Irwin county, the scene of his crime. They returned without him, stating that he had attempted to escape while in the woods and was shot down. His body was found with nineteen bullets in it, and the bushes around it were riddled with balls.

A special from Roswell Junction says: Our usual quiet community is somewhat aroused, by an attempt of rape, by a negro boy about 18 years old, known as Tom Cobb, who is working with Mr. Dave Fulcher, a farmer, living about two miles west of the place on the Roswell road.

Sunday night about 12 o'clock, Mr. Fulcher was awakenod by the screaming of one of his daughters sleeping in adjoining room with her sister, and a neighbor girl. She called her father telling him some one was in the room. He thought that they were only frightened probably from a dream, and told them to go to sleep, but they insisted and finally to pacify them, visited the room with a light, and under the bed, lay the negro Tom Cobb.
Mr. Fucher offered no act of violence but with determined coolness, arrested him, and sent for Mr. Marion Adams, a near neighbor, who assisted in guarding him until morning. They brought him to this place and was tried before Justice Elliott, and committed to Decatur jail in default of bond, to await his trial in August.

The negro offers no excuse for the act but claiming it to be somnambulism upon his part, nevertheless, he was wide awake when discovered under the bed.

Miss Fulcher says she was awakened by some one having hold of her hand. No attempt of lynching or violence has been spoken of whatever and doubtless the matter will rest quiet and allow the law to take the proper course.

A terrible railroad wreck occurred Thursday on the Savannah, Florida and Western railroad at the trestle over the Ochlocknee river, five miles from Thomasville. Freight train No. 25, consisting of four cars and the cab, had just crossed the river when about 400 feet of the trestle gave way, precipitating the entire train, except the engine, to the ground, twenty feet below. Fortunately, there were but four people on the train. The conductor and a negro brakeman were seriously injured. The negro will probably recover, but the conductor's injuries, though not necessarily fatal, are dangerous.

A special train from Thomasville was sent to the wreck as soon as possible, carrying a physician and all necessary help. The two injured men were carried to Thomasville and are doing well. The cause of the accident is not known, but the company is doing everything in its power for the men that were hurt. The cars are broken into splinters.

Amos Miller, the negro who raped Mrs. Scad in Maury county, has been caught and lodged in jail at Columbia. In an interview he admitted the deed, and told just how he accomplished it. He said that he had returned to see the daughter, who had in the meantime gone to the field with her father. He was disappointed in not finding her, but substituted the mother. There is great excitement, and it is not improbable that Miller will be lynched.

BOWLING GREEN KY. May 10
BOWLING, GREEN, KY., May 10.—During the winter J. Marion Sloss, a prominent farmer, living about three miles west of Woodburn, had the misfortune to lose nineteen head of horses and mules by death. It could not be accounted for, but the supposition was that some disease was among them. Still it seemed to Mr. Sloss quite strange that a contagious disease selected only the stock on his place and left that of his neighbor's immutable. For several months past the stock of Mr. Sloss have been free from any disease, and he had about come to the conclusion that he was not to have any more trouble in that line, but Thursday another of his horses died and two more were sick.

Having had some slight suspicion for some time, Mr. Sloss took some of the feed from the trough where his stock are fed and sent for Drs. Gardner and Duncan, who made analysis and found the food contained a large quantity of poison. For a long time one Tom Roney, of color, a resident of the Rich Pond vicinity, has been suspected of the deed, but not being desirous of doing any injury to him without being sure of his guilt, nothing was done in regard to the matter until Thursday night. This last outrage was too much for the good citizens of the community, and Thursday night at 12 o'clock a quiet, determined mob went to the home of Joe Smith, where Roney lived, and securing him, carried him to a grove one mile north of Woodbury, and hung him to the limb of a tree, from which his body was cut down Friday morning.

This is the first hanging that has taken place in Warren County for a long term of years. The mob which did the lynching was not a large mob, but went at the work systematically and determinedly, and was only a short time in getting through with the jolt and with very little noise.

Lost in a Fog.
Mr. CHANDLER is an unfortunate victim of untoward circumstances. On Thursday last he addressed the United States Senate at length on certain alleged election outrages in Louisiana at the last gubernatorial election. Column after column of the Congressional Record is filled with what purports to be a speech delivered by him and with the extracts which he caused to be read by the Clerk of the Senate whilst at intervals he rested and refreshed himself. The names and residences of the persons said to have been lynched in 1887 and 1888 are given in full—not only those lynched in Louisiana but those lynched in every southern State. Virginia heads the list with the following: "1887, July 25, REUBEN COLE at Surry Courthouse, Va." Again: Jn 1888, July 15, "WILLIAM SMITH, near Christiansburg, Va."

Let us stop to remark in passing that the dates on which these lynchings occurred in Virginia bear unimpeachable testimony that CHANDLER willfully and deliberately falsified the facts when he tried to make the Senate and the country believe that they were resorted to as a means of "suppressing the negro vote"; and we trust that Mr. DANIEL will at some opportune moment make a statement on this subject, and thus have the facts embalmed in the Congressional Record.

We say CHANDLER made a "huge" speech:

"His speech was a terrible speech indeed—Was Timothy Thady Mulligan's."

He must have occupied several hours on Thursday, after having occupied several other hours on preceding days, in setting forth the "enormities" of the southern people—their crimes, their heartlessness, their wickedness, their inhumanity. It was no doubt his intention to revolutionize the North, and convert all the Democratic States and congressional districts in that section into Republican States and congressional districts. He roared like a bull. He made himself ridiculous in the eyes of the people of the South. But all the same he raved, suppressed the truth, and endeavored "to make the worse appear the better cause."

What became of all these words?—words?—words? The telegraph devoted that night but little space comparatively to Mr. CHANDLER. He was completely overslaughed. The President of the United States had raised a fog in which CHANDLER's chatterings were lost. The Louisiana election-outrages were dwarfed into absolute insignificance by the message touching our fisheries. CHANDLER no doubt bewailed the bad luck which turned all his campaign thunder into the mutterrings and mouthings of a baffled conspirator against the peace and prosperity of the country.

Borrowing the words of The International Magazine, which once said of ELIHU BURRETT, "Let the Learned Blacksmith retire; the world wants a new humbug," we say "Let WILLIAM E. CHANDLER retire; his party needs a new clown."

The murderer was about 23 years old. Just after midnight on Saturday an orderly crowd of about 100 persons gathered near Shelby, composed of whites and blacks, on horseback and on foot. After arranging for a leader the body proceeded to the jail, overpowered the guard, and extinguished the lights. To gain entrance to the murderer's cell it was necessary to break two heavy locks, but this work seemed only play for determined men.

Upon entering the cell of the doomed man one of the lynchers told him his fate, and that resistance would be useless. He then placed a rope around the negro's neck and led him forth. When about one mile east of the jail the lynchers halted, placed the rope over the limb of a big oak, and the leader told the culprit to say his prayers. The negro showed no sign of fear. He said that the sentence of death was a just one. He spoke and prayed for several minutes, and was then pinioned sideways on the horse. In a flash the animal sped on, and the negro was swinging in mid-air, his body writhing in the agony of death. Yesterday afternoon the body was cut down and an inquest held. The verdict was: "Died of strangulation at the hands of parties unknown."

We copy from an exchange a summary of the facts in the other case which transpired about the same time as the above:

In Wharton county is a village called Spanish Camp. It is a retired and isolated spot in the edge of a dense forest. Here some negroes had gained possession of some land which they were quietly tilling and from which they had raised a crop. Some white men coveted the ground and ordered the negroes to vacate. It is rumored in Wharton that a little negro boy who knew all the parties implicated in the butchery says that there were thirteen in the party of butchers, and he has given all their names to the sheriff.

RICHMOND, Tex., March 26.—Two more colored men were killed near Spanish Camp, the scene of the recent butchery of six colored men and women. The Thursday night murders occurred on the plantation known as the Battled place. A reign of terror exists in Wharton county among the colored population. It is believed some secret society has been organized among the white planters for the purpose of expelling and killing obnoxious regressors and their white sympathizers. Among the latter is Henry Wyatt, a well-to-white farmer, who arrived here yesterday from near Spanish Camp. Ross has recently ordered a company of state rangers to report to the sheriff at Wharton for the purpose of keeping the peace and preventing bloodshed during the coming session of the district court, when it is expected a militant of assassins will be denounced before the grand jury. The presence of rangers, however, does not prevent parties whose lives are threatened, like Wyatt, from leaving the county, as they have no faith in the ability of rangers to prevent their assassination. The condition of affairs is nearly as bad as it was in Kemper county, Mississippi, twelve years ago.

BARKING UP THE WRONG TREE. The Victoria Advocate gives tongue
at the foot of the wrong persimmon when it charges the LIGHT with having dragged out the Wharton murder into the light of day for political effect, as it does in the following editorial:

"Is the San Antonio LIGHT certain that the 'recent murder of seven negroes in Wharton county' was committed by democrats and that it was the outcome of politics? If the LIGHT can prove such a thing, it need not go any further to get its campaign material for next fall. We give these pointers to the LIGHT free of charge for it will need them, and many more, to help a republican to the front when the cold, cheerless days of next November come. The truth of the matter is, the LIGHT, like the party it represents, is in the predicament of a drowning man and is grasping at a single straw. Politics or the democraey had just about as much to do with the killing as the LIGHT editor did. It occurred in a county that has, at present, a republican judge, and some of those who have been arrested for the crime are "good republicans." This it is and nothing more."

The presence of that republican judge accounts for the demand for a company of rangers, and the remonstrance against the governor's sending those rangers, demonstrates that a republican judge had a mighty hard row to hoe in bringing negro murderers to justice.

What the LIGHT did charge, does charge and must continue to charge so long as it is arraigned for its condemnation of these inhuman murders by a democratic press, is this: the democratic press of Texas did not condemn these foul murders. The journals which condemn the LIGHT for charging that a colored man's life is not as sacred in Texas as a white man's, have not raised their voices to denounce this damnable deed, but had seven white men been smoked and fired out of their cabin in the dead of night by negroes and shot in cold blood by the light of their own burning dwelling, the voice of the same journals would have cracked the very vault of heaven with the roar of its condemnation. It was not for political effect but in the cause of a common humanity that the LIGHT uttered its protest against the damnable inhumanity which refused to brand the murder as it deserved, because of the color of the skin of the poor victims. The LIGHT never mentioned, insinuated or charged that politics had anything to do with that murder and the Advocate knows it. Its reference thereto is the most miserable subterfuge. The LIGHT does say, however, that had such a murder been committed in a republican state, every journal would have branded the murder as a diabolical outrage, irrespective of the color of the skins of the murdered victims.

The Senate then proceeded to the consideration of the following preamble and resolution reported from the joint committee on the Library:

"Whereas the Italians, residents of the city of Washington and citizens of the United States, have, through the president of the society for a monument to Garibaldi, presented to the United States a life-size marble bust of that great patriot and distinguished representative citizen of Italy, Guissepe Garibaldi; and

MR. EVARTS' EULOGY.

Mr. Evarts proceeded to deliver an eulogy on the life, character, and great deeds of the Italian hero and "liberator." His peroration was as follows:

"Heroes, statesmen, lawyers, wise men, philosophers, and poets make out the long roll of ancient Roman glory; but, after all, these are for history and for scholars. But for human nature there must be found, if names are to live in the hearts and be forever on the lips of the human race, 'some touch of nature which makes the whole world kin.' And thus the name of Lucretia, whose outraged virtue could bear no less an expiation than her own life, taken by herself, and whose blood could brook no lesser vengeance than that the whole race and blood of tyrant kings should be driven from authority in Rome and a republic founded; and Cornelia, the great example of the fame and brain of Roman matrons; these throw into insignificance the pomps, and attires, and decorations of women. The mother of the Graciella stands out to all the world as the glory of woman, the mother of sons. And Horatius, who pits his own strength and his own life against the idee of war at the bridge, so as to hold it long enough to provide for the saving of the city; and Regulus, the monument of Roman faith, who was sent as an ambassador from Carthage to give advice for peace, on his promise to return if successful, and who advised the Senate, for the glory and fame of Rome, to make no peace with Carthage, and returned to Carthage, to torture and to death; these, and such names as these, are names to be remembered by the world. These are names to conjure with. And Garibaldi's inextringuishable name shall be a name to conjure with for liberty and love of country, so long as, and wherever, these great sentiments shall warm the human breast."

Mr. Evarts was greeted with the clapping of hands as he concluded his speech.
